svg.title: Compute versus communication ratio: the idealized ten-microsecond figure and the real overheads that must be measured
svg.desc: A timeline shows milliseconds of local attention and GEMM work between synchronization boundaries, against an idealized ten-microsecond serialization of 512 kilobytes at 50 gigabytes per second — labeled as a division, not a measurement. A panel lists what real synchronization adds: RDMA and collective latency, software overhead, PCIe traversal, memory access, and barrier cost. The thesis is the ratio, and it must be demonstrated on real NICs and a real switch.
svg.text: The Ratio Is the Thesis — and It Must Be Measured
Milliseconds of local work between boundaries versus hundreds of kilobytes on the wire
Between boundaries: local compute
ms-scale attention / GEMM work per node
grows with context — especially favorable toward 1M tokens
512 KB
boundary
The idealized arithmetic
400 Gb/s ≈ 50 GB/s
512 KB ÷ 50 GB/s ≈ 10 µs
⚠ a division, not a measurement
nominal link bandwidth only; no latency,
no software path, no barrier cost included
What a real sync adds

g.text: · software overhead in the runtime path

svg.text: end-to-end time is an open question, not a constant
The research hypothesis
If nodes do milliseconds of useful work between boundaries, hundreds of KB per boundary is not scary — the
compute/communication ratio carries the design. A fused schedule might cut collective time from ~25% of wall
time to ~5–10%. Both figures are hypotheses to test, not results.
Measurement plan
Demonstrate on the real NICs and switch: per-boundary bytes and latency, collective-time fraction of wall time,
barrier stalls, stragglers, switch congestion — published whatever the numbers turn out to be.
